strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving short quaternary codes for insertion, deletion, and substitution errors. Using learned geometry to guide codebook selection is a potentially useful application of distance embeddings.

Algorithm 1 excludes neighbours using exact Levenshtein distances, ensuring minimum distance three independently of embedding accuracy. Table 1 shows consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs, reaching 36,368 codewords and a 68.9% rate at length 11.

The decoding experiments provide substantial empirical evidence: retrieving four neighbours followed by exact verification produces zero observed failures in 10^8 sampled single-edit trials at each tested length. The original-versus-revised loss ablation is also useful.
The overall pipeline is understandable, a source-code repository is linked, and the manuscript acknowledges approximation errors, construction scalability, and the absence of an optimality proof.
weaknesses: The central justification for codeword selection is unsound as stated (Section 4.2): batch normalization does not imply a multivariate Gaussian embedding distribution. The manuscript provides no quantitative validation that its Gaussian-density score predicts actual Levenshtein-neighbour counts, especially after candidates are removed. The simplified binary t-SNE visualization does not establish this relationship.

The headline claim of reliable O(n) decoding is unsupported. The k=1 decoder fails on approximately 0.33–0.83% of sampled inputs, while Section 5.5 assigns O(n^2) complexity to the verified k>1 version. Zero sampled failures does not establish correction of every single-edit corruption. Moreover, the conditions needed for logarithmic expected k-d-tree queries are not established for these learned 64-dimensional embeddings.

The speed comparison uses an unnecessarily weak baseline: scanning the codebook with exact edit-distance calculations. For single-error bounded-distance decoding, one can enumerate the O(n) possible inverse edits and check codebook membership using a hash table, avoiding a full scan. The cited hardness of unrestricted edit distance does not establish hardness at this fixed error radius. Consequently, the reported speedups do not demonstrate an advantage over appropriate exact decoders.

The incremental contribution beyond the embedding methods in references [43,44] needs stronger evaluation. Random greedy selection is the only substantive construction-search baseline; comparisons with degree-based greedy packing or local improvement are missing. At length 11, the reported 16.8% cardinality improvement over random selection corresponds to about one percentage point of code rate, making these comparisons important for assessing significance.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with a redundancy curve over five short lengths supplies neither an optimality certificate nor a tight bound. The substitution-counting argument does not establish that the additional log-log term is necessary, and comparisons with asymptotically designed constructions do not establish the best achievable finite-length performance.

The application claims are not validated by the isolated-segment experiments. No mechanism or evaluation establishes how segment boundaries are recovered after insertions and deletions in concatenated streams, or what rate remains after synchronization and outer-code overhead.

Reproducibility and practical cost are insufficiently documented in the manuscript. Missing details include training-pair sampling, training budget and optimization settings, handling of variable-length corrupted inputs, and timing hardware. Construction time and peak memory are also unreported despite enumerating all 4^n candidates. The repository link is helpful, but these omissions limit assessment of the reported efficiency.
